title: Spinal accessory nerve stimulation during neck dissection (SANE)
official: Spinal accessory nerve stimulation during neck dissection (SANE): a randomised, single-blind, single-centre external pilot study
summary:
Background and study aims
People with head and neck cancer sometimes need an operation called a neck dissection to remove lymph nodes from the neck. During this operation, a nerve called the spinal accessory nerve can be stretched or injured. This nerve helps control shoulder movement, and injury can lead to shoulder pain, weakness and difficulty moving the arm. These problems can persist for many months after surgery and can affect everyday activities and ability to work. 
Research suggests that applying a small electrical current to an injured nerve during surgery may help the nerve recover. Previous studies have used 60 minutes of electrical stimulation, but this may be difficult to introduce routinely because of the additional operating time. Research suggests that a shorter period of 10 minutes may also be beneficial. 
The SANE study is a small pilot study. Its main aim is not to determine whether the treatment works, but to find out whether a larger study comparing 10 minutes of nerve stimulation with standard care can be successfully carried out in the NHS. We will assess whether patients can be recruited and followed up, whether the treatment can be delivered as planned, and whether it is acceptable to the surgical team. 

Who can participate?
We aim to recruit 14 adults aged over 18 years with head and neck cancer who are due to have a neck dissection as part of treatment intended to cure their cancer. Participants must be able and willing to provide informed consent.
People will not be able to take part if they have previously had a neck dissection, have existing neurological or shoulder problems, have an implanted electrical device such as a pacemaker, or if the spinal accessory nerve or trapezius muscle needs to be removed during surgery. 

What does the study involve?
Participants will be randomly allocated to one of two groups. One group will receive their usual NHS care. The other group will receive usual NHS care plus 10 minutes of electrical stimulation of the spinal accessory nerve during their neck dissection. The stimulation is given while the participant is under general anaesthetic. Participants will not know which group they have been allocated to. 
Before surgery, participants will complete questionnaires about their shoulder function and quality of life and undergo tests of shoulder movement and nerve function. Blood samples will also be collected to investigate biological factors that may be related to nerve injury and recovery. 
Participants will be followed up at 3, 6 and 12 months after surgery. The shoulder and nerve assessments and questionnaires will be repeated at these visits. Wherever possible, study visits will take place alongside routine hospital appointments to reduce inconvenience. 
Each participant is expected to be involved in the study for approximately 15 months, from initial telephone screening until the final 12-month follow-up. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
As this is a pilot study, it is not designed to show whether nerve stimulation improves shoulder function. Participants who receive nerve stimulation may experience improved nerve recovery and shoulder function, but this cannot be guaranteed. All participants may benefit from the additional monitoring and assessments provided during the study. The information collected will help researchers design a larger trial and may help improve care for future patients undergoing neck dissection. 
Nerve stimulation is considered low risk, and previous studies have not reported treatment-related nerve injury or damage to surrounding tissues. For participants receiving stimulation, the procedure may slightly increase the length of the operation and time under general anaesthetic. Blood tests may cause temporary discomfort, bruising or light-headedness. Tests of nerve and shoulder function may cause mild discomfort or tiredness, and some questions about health and wellbeing may be upsetting. Participants can take breaks or decline to answer questions if they wish. 

Where is the study run from?
The study is being conducted at Churchill Hospital, Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Oxford, UK. It is a single-centre study. 

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
The study is expected to start on 1 October 2026. Participant recruitment is planned from 1 January 2027 to 1 July 2027.
Participants will be followed for 12 months after surgery. The overall study is expected to run until 1 March 2030, allowing time for completion of follow-up, data collection, data checking and analysis. The study will be considered complete when the final participant's follow-up data have been entered and all outstanding data queries have been resolved. 

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by ORACLE Head & Neck Cancer UK. 

Who is the main contact?
Mr Akira Wiberg, akira.wiberg@ndorms.ox.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients in primary study:
1. Competent adult patients with head and neck cancer who are scheduled to undergo neck dissection including level 2b +/- level 5
2. Willing and able to give informed consent for participation in the trial.
3. Age >18 years, male or female
4. Surgery is intended to be curative


Healthcare professionals in qualitative sub-study:
1. Surgical consultant, surgical registrar, anaesthetic consultant, anaesthetic registrar, scrub nurse or operating department practitioner involved in the 10-min stimulation arms
2. Willing and able to give consent
Exclusion criteria:
Patients in primary study:
1. Previous neck dissection
2. Intra-operative resection of spinal accessory nerve or trapezius
3. Pre-existing neurological or shoulder dysfunction
4. Implanted electrical device e.g. pacemaker

Healthcare professionals in qualitative sub-study:
1. Lack of English language proficiency
